What I did read: Enduring Word (David Guzik, a Calvary Chapel pastor, who quotes Spurgeon, Clarke and Hiebert); Ellicott (Anglican); Gill (Baptist and Calvinist); Matthew Henry; Bob Utley on bible.org; Precept Austin; Ligonier; the Gospel Coalition; John MacArthur (gty.org); BibleHub's Q&A page; and Catholic Answers (catholic.com).

---

## 1 Peter 5 – Notes

**v. 1**
- An "elder" was an idea taken from Jewish community life. It stresses maturity and wisdom more than actual age. Peter could speak with authority because he had seen Christ suffer. "Partaker of the glory" may point back to the Transfiguration. Spurgeon is quoted: a preacher should put himself on the same level as his hearers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/
- Ellicott: the Greek word for "witness" is less about having watched and more about *testifying* to Christ's sufferings. Sharing in the glory follows naturally from witnessing the suffering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
- Gill: "elder" here means an office, not age. Being an apostle includes being an elder. Peter could have commanded but chose to plead, which shows humility. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-peter-5.html
- Utley: "fellow elder" means joint participation. Peter doesn't press his authority as an apostle. "Elder" is a Jewish term, while "overseer" came from Greek city government. https://bible.org/seriespage/i-peter-5
- **Where traditions differ (the papacy):** Several Protestant writers read this verse against the papacy.
  - Gill: Peter doesn't call himself "prince of the apostles" or "vicar of Christ," as his "pretended successor" does. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-peter-5.html
  - Matthew Henry makes the same contrast with Peter's "pretended successors." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Pe/1Pe_005.cfm
  - Guzik: Peter claimed no position "such as being the pope." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/
  - MacArthur: Peter calls himself just a fellow elder under the Chief Shepherd. https://www.gty.org/sermons/90-291/the-pope-and-the-papacy
- **Catholic view:** "Fellow elder" is Peter showing the same humility he asks of others in v. 5. Paul also played down his own status without losing his authority. Calling himself an elder doesn't cancel Peter being "first" among the apostles (Matt 10:2). https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/defending-the-papacy

**v. 2**
- Peter seems to be remembering Jesus' commission to him in John 21:15–17. A shepherd leads, guides, feeds and protects. "Overseer" means a manager or supervisor. "Willingly" means serving out of love, not as a forced job. "Not for greed" means money must not be the motive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/
- Ellicott:
  - "Shepherd" is the John 21:16 verb and covers the whole work of governing, not just feeding.
  - He thinks the warning is mainly against leaders abandoning their post out of fear of persecution, like hired hands.
  - "Greed" warns against staying in office for the pay, or threatening to resign unless paid more.
  - He describes Peter as the one "to whom the flock throughout the whole world was committed."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
- Precept Austin: this doesn't forbid fair pay ("the laborer is worthy of his wages"). It forbids taking up the work for gain, whether money, prestige or power. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1peter_verse_by_verse_51-14
- Utley: "elders," "overseers/bishops" and "shepherds/pastors" seem to be used interchangeably. Ancient manuscripts disagree on whether the words "exercising oversight" belong in the text. https://bible.org/seriespage/i-peter-5

**v. 3**
- Guzik: the sheep are entrusted to the shepherds, not owned by them. The warning against "lording it" shows elders really did have authority that could be abused. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/
- Precept Austin: shepherds should lead as examples, not drive the flock as dictators. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1peter_verse_by_verse_51-14
- Henry: the people are God's heritage and should be treated with meekness and tenderness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Pe/1Pe_005.cfm
- **Where traditions differ (church government):**
  - Ellicott (Anglican) says that in one sense church leaders "are, and ought to be, lords and princes over the rest." What is forbidden is acting like tyrants. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
  - Gill (Baptist) says the Greek word here (*klēros*, the root of "clergy") belongs to all the saints, not to a special class of officers. He rejects reading it as priests and deacons under bishops. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-peter-5.html

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: the word "Chief Shepherd" seems to have been coined by Peter. "Unfading" suggests an amaranth crown, made from a flower that keeps its colour. Peter adds "of glory" so it isn't taken too literally. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
- Guzik: pastors answer to the Chief Shepherd for *His* flock. The crown is unlike the fading wreath of an Olympic winner. Crowns are promised to all faithful believers, not only shepherds. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/
- Gill: Christ is Chief Shepherd. All other pastors get their commission and gifts from him and answer to him. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-peter-5.html
- Henry: Peter sets this crown against the "filthy lucre" (greed) of v. 2. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Pe/1Pe_005.cfm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: the command starts with the young but applies to "all." "Clothe yourselves" uses a rare word for a slave putting on an apron, as Jesus did at the foot-washing. The quotation is from Proverbs 3:34. Hiebert is quoted: God sets himself "in battle array" against the proud. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/
- Ellicott: the word means to tie humility on tightly, like a slave's cape, a badge of servitude. "None are to be masters" in the church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
- Gill: humility is part of the believer's clothing of sanctification. It is *not* the robe of justifying righteousness. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-peter-5.html
- **Who are the "younger"? Readings differ:**
  - Ellicott: most naturally all lay people compared with the presbyters. He also allows that it could mean lower clergy, such as deacons and readers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
  - Gill: all ordinary church members as distinct from their officers. He insists there are no lower offices besides deacons. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-peter-5.html
  - Utley: "younger" points to a real age contrast, so "elders" here plays on both age and office. https://bible.org/seriespage/i-peter-5
- Precept Austin collects devotional quotations: humility is the clearest evidence of saving faith, and the humble heart "can hold most grace." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_peter_54-5

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: "God's mighty hand" means a protecting shelter, not a punishing hand. "In due time" probably means the Day of Judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
- Gill: humbling yourself means submitting to affliction without complaining. Being under God's hand is safe. God may lift people up in this life, and always does in the next. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-peter/5-6.html
- Guzik: God knows the right time to lift us up better than we do. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/
- Utley: this echoes Matthew 23:12 and James 4. God regularly resists the proud and lifts the lowly. https://bible.org/seriespage/i-peter-5
- A writer quoted on Precept Austin: Peter is not saying we can manipulate God into blessing us by humbling ourselves. God "does not get involved in a merit system." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_peter_56-7

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: an adaptation of Psalm 55:22 (Greek version). Anxiety implies distrust of God and a belief that we can manage better ourselves. The two "cares" in the English are different Greek words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
- Guzik:
  - Casting cares on God is itself a sign of humility.
  - "Casting" is energetic: throw it away from you, using the "two hands" of prayer and faith.
  - Some worries can't be cast on God because they are ungodly, such as wanting to be rich or famous.
  - A Christian full of worry reflects badly on their Father.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/
- Precept Austin: the Lord is our "Care-taker." Our part is to obey, and God carries the rest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_peter_56-7

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: the commands are urgent. The picture is a shepherd who spots a lion near the flock while the guards doze. The roar signals hunger. Satan is singling out individuals, especially in times of persecution. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
- Guzik: Satan has not yet been bound (Rev 20). He was "de-fanged" at the cross (Col 2:15), but his lies can still devour. Spurgeon is quoted: Satan may use pleasant "sweets" as well as hardships. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/
- Henry: Satan stirs up persecution to drive believers to give up their faith. Being self-controlled means holding worldly things loosely. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Pe/1Pe_005.cfm

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: "stand and face him" rather than running from duty. The church should present a united front. The same sufferings are "being inflicted" on the worldwide brotherhood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
- Guzik: Hiebert is quoted: Scripture never tells believers to flee from the devil. "Resist" means "stand against." Spurgeon is quoted: Satan becomes a dog that drives the sheep nearer to Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/
- Gill: resist by firmly holding to the faith. Don't be surprised by sufferings that other Christians share. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/5-9.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott:
  - The best text reads "called *you*."
  - "A little while" stresses that all time is short.
  - The verbs are future: a promise.
  - "Restore" means mending what is broken.
  - He quotes Bengel's explanation of the verbs.
  - He thinks Peter expected the persecution to end before the world did.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
- Guzik: Peter ends with prayer, having learned not to rely on his own strength. God uses suffering to perfect us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/
- **Doctrinal angle:** Gill says "perfect" here means sanctification, not justification, which is already complete in Christ. Sanctification grows by degrees, and even the best believers are not perfect in this life. He reads the verse as a prayer of faith or a promise. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-peter/5-10.html (Methodist "Christian perfection" readings: not found.)
- Henry: only "the God of all grace" can keep believers persevering, so seek him in prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Pe/1Pe_005.cfm

**v. 11**
- Ellicott quotes Leighton: Peter adds praise to his prayer. If the dominion is God's, what is there to fear? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
- Guzik: God is worthy of praise for doing this work in us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. "As I regard him" may vouch for Silas to Jewish Christians who were uneasy about him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_peter/5.htm
- Guzik: Silvanus probably wrote down most of the letter, and these closing lines are in Peter's own hand. Grace is the believer's present standing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-5/
- Utley: following E. R. Richards, "through Silvanus" probably means Silvanus *carried* the letter rather than wrote it. "True grace" means the one true gospel. "Stand firm" links back to v. 9. https://bible.org/seriespage/i-peter-5

**v. 13**
- **"Babylon" as Rome (the majority view):**
  - Ligonier: most likely the church at Rome. It continues the theme of the church as exiled true Israel. Peter calling Mark "son" suggests Peter led Mark to faith and supports Mark's Gospel coming from Peter. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/silvanus
  - The Gospel Coalition: "almost certainly" Rome. https://au.thegospelcoalition.org/article/gods-elect-resident-aliens-in-babylon/
  - Utley: a coded name for Rome (compare Rev 14, 17–18). "She" is the church, which Scripture pictures as female. "Mark" is John Mark. https://bible.org/seriespage/i-peter-5
  - BibleHub Q&A: Rome. No tradition places Peter in Mesopotamia. Mark was in Rome. It also carries an exile theme. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_does_Peter_mention_Babylon_in_1_Peter.htm
- **Minority readings:** BibleHub's 5:13 page says the Greek is just "the co-elect one" (feminine), and some have taken her to be Peter's wife. One excerpt there argues for literal Babylon from the order in which Peter lists the provinces. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/5-13.htm
- **Catholic view:** "Babylon" is evidence that Peter was in Rome, which supports Catholic claims about the bishop of Rome. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/defending-the-papacy

**v. 14**
- The page text I reached broke off before the comments on this verse. Nothing found beyond the text itself.
